claim: Myogenic progenitor cells migrate to the final myogenic sites while being segregated and patterned into discrete muscle masses in coordination with the development of other CNC-derived craniofacial connective tissues.
source: Later, in coordination with the development of other CNC-derived craniofacial connective tissues, myogenic progenitor cells in these mesodermal cores migrate to the final myogenic sites while being segregated and patterned into discrete muscle masses (Noden and Francis-West, 2006; Sambasivan et al., 2011; Shih et al., 2008; Ziermann et al., 2018).

claim: A distinct regulatory network upstream of myogenesis has been identified during early-stage pharyngeal muscle development.

claim: The first and second pharyngeal arch mesodermal cores respectively contribute to the muscles responsible for mastication and facial expression.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

source: From E13.5 onwards, individual soft palatal muscles, particularly the levator veli palatini (LVP), can be clearly detected segregating from the rest of the pharyngeal muscles and populating the soft palate primordium, patterning and migrating towards the midline in parallel to the lateral-to-medial outgrowth of the connective tissues consisting of the CNC-derived palatal mesenchymal cells (Grimaldi et al., 2015; Han et al., 2021; Li et al., 2019).

claim: Soft palatal muscle development provides an optimal opportunity to study the initiation, segregation, and migration of muscle anlage formation during craniofacial development.
source: Therefore, soft palatal muscle development provides an optimal opportunity to study the initiation, segregation, and migration of muscle anlage formation during craniofacial development.

claim: The most common congenital craniofacial malformation is cleft lip with or without cleft palate.
source: Clinically, the most common congenital craniofacial malformation is cleft lip with or without cleft palate (Vyas et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: When the soft palate is affected, disruption of the soft palatal shelves separating the oral and nasal cavities co-occurs with defects in soft palatal muscle formation and oropharyngeal function.
source: When the soft palate is affected, disruption of the soft palatal shelves separating the oral and nasal cavities co-occurs with defects in soft palatal muscle formation and oropharyngeal function (Li et al., 2019; Carvajal Monroy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Loss of key regulators in the perimysial cells ultimately affects soft palatal muscle differentiation and patterning in mouse models.
source: Furthermore, mouse models have demonstrated that loss of key regulators in the perimysial cells, a subset of the palatal mesenchymal connective tissues closely associated with the muscles, ultimately affects soft palatal muscle differentiation and patterning (Han et al., 2021; Sugii et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CNC-derived perimysial cells possibly contribute to part of the embryonic myogenic niche for craniofacial muscle development at the later stages.
source: These findings suggest that CNC-derived perimysial cells possibly contribute to part of the embryonic myogenic niche for craniofacial muscle development at the later stages.

source: Thus, soft palate development can serve as a useful model for studying how perimysial cells regulate late pharyngeal muscle anlage formation through tissue-tissue interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the characteristics of soft palate development.

claim: TGF-β signaling is a predominant and specific signaling activity that enables the perimysial cells to interact with the adjacent myogenic cells during late pharyngeal muscle development.
source: Using unbiased single-cell RNAseq (scRNAseq) data analysis combined with mouse genetic approaches, we identified TGF-β signaling as a predominant and specific signaling activity that enables the perimysial cells to interact with the adjacent myogenic cells during late pharyngeal muscle development.
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis and mouse genetic approaches.

claim: Creb5 cooperates with TGF-β signaling to co-activate the expression of specific perimysial-to-myogenic signals such as Fgf18 to regulate pharyngeal myogenesis.
source: Furthermore, we identified that a perimysial regulator Creb5 cooperates with TGF-β signaling to co-activate the expression of specific perimysial-to-myogenic signals such as Fgf18 to regulate pharyngeal myogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: TGF-β signaling and perimysial-specific regulators may cooperatively define perimysial-to-myogenic signals in regulating pharyngeal myogenesis.
source: Taken together, our findings reveal that TGF-β signaling and perimysial-specific regulators may cooperatively define perimysial-to-myogenic signals in regulating pharyngeal myogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on the findings presented in the study.

claim: The morphologically homologous palatal mesenchyme is patterned into heterogeneous cellular domains associated with distinct anatomical locations and gene expression profiles during late pharyngeal muscle development.
source: In parallel, during this stage, our recent scRNAseq analysis identified that the morphologically homologous palatal mesenchyme is also patterned into heterogeneous cellular domains associated with distinct anatomical locations and gene expression profiles (Han et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous scRNAseq analysis.

claim: The perimysial population, anatomically adjacent to the myogenic cells, serves as a microenvironment or niche for embryonic pharyngeal muscle development.
source: We thus hypothesized that the perimysial population, anatomically adjacent to the myogenic cells, serves as a microenvironment or niche for embryonic pharyngeal muscle development.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on anatomical observations.

claim: There must be a specific regulatory mechanism that differentiates the perimysial cells from the rest of the palatal mesenchymal cell populations so that the perimysial cells can provide specific signals to define the myogenic site.
source: Furthermore, there must be a specific regulatory mechanism that differentiates the perimysial cells from the rest of the palatal mesenchymal cell populations so that the perimysial cells can provide specific signals to define the myogenic site.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on logical reasoning.

claim: Signaling pathways play critical roles in the patterning and fate determination of craniofacial mesenchymal cells.
source: Since signaling pathways have been reported to play critical roles in the patterning and fate determination of craniofacial mesenchymal cells (Mishina and Snider, 2014; Neubüser et al., 1997; Vincentz et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2019), we performed an unbiased signaling activity analysis of the cell populations of the soft palate, focusing on identifying key signaling pathways specifically activated in the perimysial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The signaling activity of all the palatal mesenchymal cell types was categorized into the same group due to the shared expression of similar signaling pathways.
source: Notably, the signaling activity of all the palatal mesenchymal cell types was categorized into the same group due to the shared expression of similar signaling pathways (Figure 1B), consistent with their common connective tissue identity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ephrin-Eph (EphA/EphB), non-canonical Wnt (ncWnt), IGF, TGF-β, FGF, and Hedgehog signaling pathways were previously identified to be required for the development of craniofacial mesenchymal tissues including palatal mesenchyme.
source: Among this group of pathways, Ephrin-Eph (EphA/EphB) (Benson and Serrano, 2012; Xavier et al., 2016), non-canonical Wnt (ncWnt) (Reynolds et al., 2019), IGF (Marchant et al., 2020), TGF-β (Iwata et al., 2011), FGF (Nie et al., 2006), and Hedgehog signaling (HH) pathways (Everson et al., 2018) were previously identified to be required for the development of craniofacial mesenchymal tissues including palatal mesenchyme, so we reasoned that they are more likely to be functionally required by the perimysial cell fate determination, too.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The TGF-β signaling activity was inferred to be the highest in the perimysial cells among the pathways analyzed.
source: We thus next analyzed the intensities of activities of these pathways in the perimysial cells and found that the TGF-β signaling activity was inferred to be the highest (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Tgfbi (transforming growth factor-beta-induced protein) was among the top 10 conserved marker genes for the perimysial cells across various developmental stages.
source: Moreover, a known TGF-β signaling downstream target, Tgfbi (transforming growth factor-beta-induced protein), was among the top 10 conserved marker genes for the perimysial cells across various developmental stages (Figure 1D), suggesting that TGF-β signaling is not only a predominant signaling pathway but also specifically associated with regulating the perimysial cell fate and maintaining a perimysial-derived signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TGF-β signaling is not only a predominant signaling pathway but also specifically associated with regulating the perimysial cell fate and maintaining a perimysial-derived signal.
source: Moreover, a known TGF-β signaling downstream target, Tgfbi (transforming growth factor-beta-induced protein), was among the top 10 conserved marker genes for the perimysial cells across various developmental stages (Figure 1D), suggesting that TGF-β signaling is not only a predominant signaling pathway but also specifically associated with regulating the perimysial cell fate and maintaining a perimysial-derived signal.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TGF-β signaling was present in the palatal shelf mesenchyme primordium during soft palatal development from E12.5 onwards.
source: Consistent with scRNAseq analysis, TGF-β signaling was present in the palatal shelf mesenchyme primordium during soft palatal development from E12.5 onwards (Figure 2A–H) and was most active in the cells surrounding the LVP myogenic cells, anatomically identified as perimysial cells (Figure 2J–L and N–P), particularly during the early segregation and separation process at E13.5 (Figure 2B, F, J, and N) and E14.5 (Figure 2C, G, K, and O).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TGF-β signaling was most active in the cells surrounding the LVP myogenic cells, anatomically identified as perimysial cells, particularly during the early segregation and separation process at E13.5 and E14.5.
source: Consistent with scRNAseq analysis, TGF-β signaling was present in the palatal shelf mesenchyme primordium during soft palatal development from E12.5 onwards (Figure 2A–H) and was most active in the cells surrounding the LVP myogenic cells, anatomically identified as perimysial cells (Figure 2J–L and N–P), particularly during the early segregation and separation process at E13.5 (Figure 2B, F, J, and N) and E14.5 (Figure 2C, G, K, and O).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TGF-β signaling was ubiquitous in the mesenchymal cells close to the pharyngeal wall at E12.5 prior to the arrival of myogenic cells.
source: Notably, TGF-β signaling was ubiquitous in the mesenchymal cells close to the pharyngeal wall at E12.5 prior to the arrival of myogenic cells (Figure 2A, E, I, and M).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The specific activation of TGF-β signaling in the presence of perimysial cells suggests that TGF-β signaling may play a role in patterning perimysial cells to establish a myogenic niche in the specific anatomical location for the LVP.
source: This specific activation of TGF-β signaling in the presence of perimysial cells suggested that TGF-β signaling may play a role in patterning perimysial cells to establish a myogenic niche in the specific anatomical location for the LVP.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed pattern of TGF-β signaling activation.

claim: Loss of TGF-β in Wnt1-Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice in the early pre-migratory neural crest cells and their derivatives from E9.5 onward affects proliferation and differentiation of the tongue and other craniofacial muscles.
source: This postulation is supported by our previous work, which showed that loss of TGF-β in Wnt1-Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice in the early pre-migratory neural crest cells and their derivatives from E9.5 onward affect proliferation and differentiation of the tongue and other craniofacial muscles (Chai et al., 2000; Han et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The perimysial cells contain at least two distinct subpopulations with different differentiation statuses: earlier perimysial progenitors (Aldh1a2+) and more committed perimysial fibroblasts.
source: E13.5-E15.5 soft palatal scRNAseq analysis led to the inference that the perimysial cells contain at least two distinct subpopulations with different differentiation statuses, namely earlier perimysial progenitors (Aldh1a2+) and more committed perimysial fibroblasts, which express markers other than Aldh1a2, such as Tbx15 (Han et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from scRNAseq analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: Aldh1a2+ perimysial progenitors are located at the base of the palatal shelf and closer to the middle pharyngeal constrictor myogenic sites outside the palatal shelf, with little overlap with the pSmad2+ area.
source: The Aldh1a2+population was located at the base of the palatal shelf and closer to the middle pharyngeal constrictor myogenic sites outside the palatal shelf; it had little overlap with the pSmad2+ area (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Smoc2 was more extensively expressed and overlapped at the periphery of the pSmad2 expression area, almost complementary to the Tbx15+ domain.
source: Smoc2 was more extensively expressed and overlapped at the periphery of the pSmad2 expression area, almost complementary to the Tbx15+ domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overlap between TGF-β signaling activity and the Tbx15+ and Smoc2+ populations suggests that TGF-β signaling may be a more specific regulator for the later stage of perimysial cells (perimysial fibroblasts), not the perimysial progenitors.
source: This overlap between TGF-β signaling activity and the Tbx15+ and Smoc2+ populations suggested that TGF-β signaling may be a more specific regulator for the later stage of perimysial cells (perimysial fibroblasts), not the perimysial progenitors.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed overlap patterns.

claim: Osr2Cre can specifically label the palatal mesenchyme without affecting the myogenic cells during soft palatal muscle development.
source: Using Osr2Cre;Rosa26LSL-tdTomato mice, we confirmed that Osr2Cre can specifically label the palatal mesenchyme without affecting the myogenic cells during soft palatal muscle development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of TGF-β signaling in the palatal mesenchyme led to morphologically deformed palatal shelves and cleft palate in the LVP region in E18.5 Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice.
source: Loss of TGF-β signaling in the palatal mesenchyme, including the perimysial cells, led to morphologically deformed palatal shelves and cleft palate in the LVP region in E18.5 Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice (Figure 3B and D), compared with the intact control palatal shelves (Figure 3A and C), indicating intrinsic defects in the palatal mesenchymal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the defective palatal shelves of Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice, LVP formation was so severely affected that no muscle fibers could be detected at E18.5.
source: In addition, while abundant MHC+ muscle fibers were present in the control palatal shelves (Figure 3E, I, G, and K), in the defective palatal shelves of Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice, LVP formation was so severely affected that no muscle fibers could be detected at this stage (Figure 3F, J, H, and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: TGF-β signaling is indispensable for the perimysial-derived signaling for myogenesis.
source: This confirmed that TGF-β signaling is indispensable for the perimysial-derived signaling for myogenesis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the severe muscle defects observed in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice.

claim: The palatal shelves of Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice started to appear morphologically different from those of the controls at around E14.5.
source: We found that the palatal shelves of Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice started to appear morphologically different from those of the controls at around E14.5, suggesting that defects in the palatal mesenchymal cells start at this stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The myogenic defects could be observed as early as E13.5 in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice while the palatal shelves remained comparable between Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl and control mice.
source: However, the myogenic defects could be observed as early as E13.5 in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice while the palatal shelves remained comparable between Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl and control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Fewer myogenic cells were present in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice compared to the control at E13.5, suggesting a defect affecting the migration of the myogenic cells.
source: As myogenic cells began to enter the palatal shelves at E13.5, fewer myogenic cells were present in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice compared to the control (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, E, and I), suggesting a defect affecting the migration of the myogenic cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: At E14.0, the reduced population of myogenic cells showed significantly less proliferative activity in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice.
source: At E14.0, this reduced population of myogenic cells also showed significantly less proliferative activity in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C, F–G, and J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by BrdU labeling data and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: No apoptosis was observed in either the control or Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl myogenic cells at E14.0.
source: No apoptosis was observed in either the control or Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl myogenic cells at E14.0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Caspase 3 staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: At E14.5, myogenic cells were still present in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice, although fewer in number than in the control.
source: At E14.5, myogenic cells were still present in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice, although fewer in number than in the control (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: From E14.5 onward, the palatal mesenchymal defects became more exacerbated over time, and the myogenic defect also increased in severity over time as myogenic progenitor cells became almost undetectable from around E16.5.
source: From E14.5 onward, the palatal mesenchymal defects became more exacerbated over time, and the myogenic defect also increased in severity over time as myogenic progenitor cells became almost undetectable from around E16.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The TGF-β signaling activity (pSmad2) was reduced in the perimysial cells adjacent to the LVP in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice.
source: We also confirmed that the TGF-β signaling activity (pSmad2) was reduced in the perimysial cells adjacent to the LVP in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2J–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of TGF-β signaling activity in the palatal mesenchyme leads to migration and proliferation defects of LVP myogenic cells in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice through cell-cell interaction.
source: Taken together, our results indicated that loss of TGF-β signaling activity in the palatal mesenchyme leads to migration and proliferation defects of LVP myogenic cells in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice through cell-cell interaction.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed defects in myogenic cells.

claim: Expression of perimysial fibroblast markers Tbx15 and Smoc2 was reduced in the perimysial population in E14.5 Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl soft palates relative to controls.
source: Consistent with the overlapping of perimysial fibroblast populations in the region of active TGF-β signaling, in our scRNAseq data we found reduced expression of perimysial fibroblast markers Tbx15 and Smoc2 in the perimysial population in E14.5 Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl soft palates relative to controls (Figure 4B and C), while the Aldh1a2+ perimysial progenitor subpopulation was not affected (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Aldh1a2+ perimysial progenitor subpopulation was not affected in E14.5 Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl soft palates.
source: Consistent with the overlapping of perimysial fibroblast populations in the region of active TGF-β signaling, in our scRNAseq data we found reduced expression of perimysial fibroblast markers Tbx15 and Smoc2 in the perimysial population in E14.5 Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl soft palates relative to controls (Figure 4B and C), while the Aldh1a2+ perimysial progenitor subpopulation was not affected (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Tbx15+ cells were located predominantly in between the LVP myogenic cells.
source: More specifically, in vivo expression patterns further showed that Tbx15+ cells were located predominantly in between the LVP myogenic cells, while Smoc2 expression was present mostly around the periphery of the myogenic site (Figure 4F and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Smoc2 expression was present mostly around the periphery of the myogenic site.
source: More specifically, in vivo expression patterns further showed that Tbx15+ cells were located predominantly in between the LVP myogenic cells, while Smoc2 expression was present mostly around the periphery of the myogenic site (Figure 4F and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Expression of Tbx15 and Smoc2 was affected in perimysial cells in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice at their respective sites.
source: Consistent with the scRNAseq analysis, expression of Tbx15 and Smoc2 was affected in perimysial cells in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice at these respective sites (Figure 4G and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Aldh1a2+ cells located mainly adjacent to the middle pharyngeal constrictor in the control were not affected in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice.
source: Also consistent with the scRNAseq analysis, the Aldh1a2+ cells located mainly adjacent to the middle pharyngeal constrictor in the control were not affected in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Runx2 is a regulator of Aldh1a2+ early perimysial progenitors.
source: While our recent study showed that Runx2 is a regulator of Aldh1a2+ early perimysial progenitors (Han et al., 2021), here we identified TGF-β signaling as the main regulator for the fate determination of both populations of the more committed perimysial fibroblasts, suggesting a specific role of TGF-β signaling in late stage-pharyngeal muscle development.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: TGF-β signaling is the main regulator for the fate determination of both populations of the more committed perimysial fibroblasts.
source: While our recent study showed that Runx2 is a regulator of Aldh1a2+ early perimysial progenitors (Han et al., 2021), here we identified TGF-β signaling as the main regulator for the fate determination of both populations of the more committed perimysial fibroblasts, suggesting a specific role of TGF-β signaling in late stage-pharyngeal muscle development.
evidence: The claim is supported by the findings presented in the study.

claim: TGF-β signaling has a specific role in late stage-pharyngeal muscle development.
source: While our recent study showed that Runx2 is a regulator of Aldh1a2+ early perimysial progenitors (Han et al., 2021), here we identified TGF-β signaling as the main regulator for the fate determination of both populations of the more committed perimysial fibroblasts, suggesting a specific role of TGF-β signaling in late stage-pharyngeal muscle development.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the findings presented in the study.

claim: Tbx15 expression was not detectable at E13.5, and only starting to be activated at a low level by a few cells at E14.0 in both control and Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice.
source: We found that Tbx15 expression was not activated at early stages: Tbx15 was not detectable E13.5, and only starting to be activated at a low level by a few cells at E14.0 in both and Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The low level of Tbx15 increased dramatically at E14.5 in the control but failed to increase in a similar manner in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice, suggesting that the reduced Tbx15 expression at E14.5 was due to a failure of activating the differentiation of Tbx15+ cells.
source: This low level of Tbx15 increased dramatically at E14.5 in the control (Figure 4F) but failed to increase in a similar manner in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice (Figure 4G), suggesting that the reduced Tbx15 expression at E14.5 was due to a failure of activating the differentiation of Tbx15+ cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed expression patterns shown in Figure 4.

claim: Smoc2 was expressed extensively in the palatal mesenchyme at E13.5 at comparable levels in control and Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice, and its expression started to reduce in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice at E14.0.
source: In parallel, we found that Smoc2 was expressed extensively in the palatal mesenchyme at E13.5 at comparable levels in control and Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice, and its expression started to reduce in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice at E14.0 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The proliferation rate in the palatal shelves and the Smoc2+ cells were not affected at E13.5 in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice.
source: Since the proliferation rate in the palatal shelves and the Smoc2+ cells were not affected at E13.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K–P), and very few cells were apoptotic in the palatal mesenchyme (less than 1%) in both the control and Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice at this stage (Figure 4—figure supplement 2Q–R), we inferred that the loss of Smoc2 was likely due to the differentiation defect of the Smoc2 populations, too.
evidence: The claim is supported by BrdU labeling data and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Very few cells were apoptotic in the palatal mesenchyme (less than 1%) in both the control and Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice at E13.5.
source: Since the proliferation rate in the palatal shelves and the Smoc2+ cells were not affected at E13.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K–P), and very few cells were apoptotic in the palatal mesenchyme (less than 1%) in both the control and Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice at this stage (Figure 4—figure supplement 2Q–R), we inferred that the loss of Smoc2 was likely due to the differentiation defect of the Smoc2 populations, too.
evidence: The claim is supported by Caspase 3 staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The loss of Smoc2 was likely due to the differentiation defect of the Smoc2 populations.
source: Since the proliferation rate in the palatal shelves and the Smoc2+ cells were not affected at E13.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K–P), and very few cells were apoptotic in the palatal mesenchyme (less than 1%) in both the control and Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice at this stage (Figure 4—figure supplement 2Q–R), we inferred that the loss of Smoc2 was likely due to the differentiation defect of the Smoc2 populations, too.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed data.

claim: TGF-β signaling is required for the fate determination of both Tbx15+ and Smoc2+ perimysial fibroblasts during early palatal mesenchyme development.
source: Thus, we concluded that TGF-β signaling is required for the fate determination of both Tbx15+ and Smoc2+ perimysial fibroblasts during early palatal mesenchyme development.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the findings presented in the study.

claim: Several enriched interactions were detected between perimysial-derived signaling molecules in ncWnt, FGF, Notch, and BMP signaling pathways (Wnt5a, Fgf18, Dlk1, and Bmp4) and corresponding receptors expressed in the myogenic cells (Fdz4, Fgfr1/4, Notch3, and Bmpr1a/Acvr2b, respectively).
source: In doing so, we detected several enriched interactions including those between perimysial-derived signaling molecules in ncWnt, FGF, Notch, and BMP signaling pathways (Wnt5a, Fgf18, Dlk1, and Bmp4) and corresponding receptors expressed in the myogenic cells (Fdz4, Fgfr1/4, Notch3, and Bmpr1a/Acvr2b, respectively) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Other interactions that may be associated with cell behavior through modulating extra-cellular matrices were identified, such as Thrombospondin (Thbs3-Sdc1), Pleiotrophin (Ptn-Ncl), Nectins (Nectin3-Nectin1), Midkine (Mdk-Ncl), and Laminins (Lama4/b1/c1-Dag1).
source: We also identified other interactions that may be associated with cell behavior through modulating extra-cellular matrices, such as Thrombospondin (Thbs3-Sdc1), Pleiotrophin (Ptn-Ncl), Nectins (Nectin3-Nectin1), Midkine (Mdk-Ncl), and Laminins (Lama4/b1/c1-Dag1) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Lama4, Fgf18, and Dlk1 are the top three molecules more enriched in the perimysial fibroblasts than in other cells.
source: By checking the expression patterns of these signaling molecules in E13.5-E15.5 soft palatal scRNAseq data, we found that Lama4, Fgf18, and Dlk1 are the top three molecules more enriched in the perimysial fibroblasts than in other cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of Fgf18 and Lama4 was found to be reduced in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl perimysial cells, whereas Dlk1 expression appeared unaffected.
source: Among these three molecules, expression of Fgf18 and Lama4 was found to be reduced in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl perimysial cells, whereas Dlk1 expression appeared unaffected (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: TGF-β signaling could regulate the expression of perimysial-derived Lama4 and Fgf18 during muscle development.
source: This suggests that TGF-β signaling could also regulate the expression of perimysial-derived Lama4 and Fgf18 during muscle development.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed reduction of Fgf18 and Lama4 in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice.

claim: Fgf18 expression is more restricted to the region of perimysial fibroblasts than that of Lama4.
source: In vivo expression of these two genes further showed that Fgf18 expression is more restricted to the region of perimysial fibroblasts (Figure 5H) than that of Lama4 (Figure 5I), similar to the TGF-β signaling activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Fgf18 is the most likely perimysial-to-myogenic signal regulated by TGF-β signaling to support myogenesis.
source: Thus, we identified Fgf18 as the most likely perimysial-to-myogenic signal regulated by TGF-β signaling to support myogenesis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the expression patterns and regulation of Fgf18.

claim: Fgf18 expression in perimysial fibroblasts is consistently enriched in the location most adjacent to the myogenic cells between E13.5-E16.5.
source: We found consistently enriched expression of Fgf18 in the location of perimysial fibroblasts most adjacent to the myogenic cells between E13.5-E16.5 (Figure 5J–K, N–O, and R–S).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The expression of Fgf18 in Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice was reduced compared to the controls.
source: Consistent with the scRNAseq analysis, the expression of Fgf18 in similar locations in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice was reduced compared to the ones in controls (Figure 5L–M, P–Q, and T–W).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and quantification shown in Figure 5.

claim: The reduction of Fgf18 expression occurred as early as E13.5, during which the defect was apparent in the myogenic cells but not in the palatal mesenchyme, suggesting TGF-β signaling regulates Fgf18 expression prior to changes to the perimysial cell fates.
source: This reduction of Fgf18 expression occurred as early as E13.5, during which the defect was apparent in the myogenic cells but not in the palatal mesenchyme, suggesting TGF-β signaling regulates Fgf18 expression prior to changes to the perimysial cell fates (Figure 5J–M and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, C, E, and G).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the timing of Fgf18 reduction and myogenic defects.

claim: The reduction of the myogenic cells was correlated with the loss of Fgf18 expression.
source: Notably, the reduction of the myogenic cells was correlated with the loss of Fgf18 expression.
evidence: The claim is based on the observed correlation between Fgf18 expression and myogenic cell numbers.

claim: In the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl soft palate at E14.5, a reduced number of Myod1+ myogenic cells was detectable in the location of the remnant Fgf18 expression compared with the presence of myogenic cells in control.
source: In the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl soft palate at E14.5, a reduced number of Myod1+ myogenic cells was detectable in the location of the remnant Fgf18 expression compared with the presence of myogenic cells in control (Figure 5O and Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5.

claim: At E16.5, the Myod1 expression became undetectable as Fgf18 expression disappeared compared with the abundant presence of both signals in the control.
source: Further, at E16.5, the Myod1 expression became undetectable as Fgf18 expression disappeared compared with the abundant presence of both signals in the control (Figure 5R–U).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The strong correlation between the perimysial-fibroblast-derived Fgf18 and Myod1+ myogenic cells supports the potential role of Fgf18 in myogenesis.
source: This strong correlation between the perimysial-fibroblast-derived Fgf18 and Myod1+ myogenic cells further supported the potential role of Fgf18 in myogenesis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed correlation.

claim: Perimysial fibroblast-derived Fgf18 signals were more likely to communicate with Fgfr1 and/or Fgfr4 in the myogenic cells, which did not express Fgfr2 or Fgfr3.
source: Consistent with CellChat predictions, perimysial fibroblast-derived Fgf18 signals were more likely to communicate with Fgfr1 and/or Fgfr4 in the myogenic cells, which did not express Fgfr2 or Fgfr3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C, F, and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fgfr1 is expressed extensively in the palatal mesenchymal cells and weakly in myogenic cells.
source: Though Fgfr1 is expressed extensively in the palatal mesenchymal cells and weakly in myogenic cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and E), Fgfr4 showed more specific and stronger expression in the myogenic cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fgfr4 showed more specific and stronger expression in the myogenic cells.
source: Though Fgfr1 is expressed extensively in the palatal mesenchymal cells and weakly in myogenic cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and E), Fgfr4 showed more specific and stronger expression in the myogenic cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fgfr4 expression was mostly enriched in the myogenic cells expressing early myogenic markers Myf5 and Pax7, but not in the more differentiated cells (Myog+/Myl1+).
source: We found that Fgfr4 expression was mostly enriched in the myogenic cells expressing early myogenic markers Myf5 and Pax7 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–K), but not in the more differentiated cells (Myog+/Myl1+) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1L and M).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myogenic progenitor cells expressing Fgfr4 also expressed the proliferative marker Mki67, consistent with the proliferative status of myogenic progenitors.
source: Interestingly, these myogenic progenitor cells also expressed the proliferative marker Mki67 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1N), consistent with the proliferative status of myogenic progenitors.
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myf5+ cells co-expressed Fgfr4 in the palatal shelf sections in vivo.
source: Consistent with the scRNAseq analysis, Myf5+ cells co-expressed Fgfr4 in the palatal shelf sections in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 1O and P).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Perimysial-fibroblast-derived Fgf18 may signal to Fgfr4 in the myogenic progenitors to orchestrate myogenic cell fate and promote their proliferation.
source: Thus, perimysial-fibroblast-derived Fgf18 may signal to Fgfr4 in the myogenic progenitors to orchestrate myogenic cell fate and promote their proliferation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the expression patterns of Fgf18 and Fgfr4.

claim: Several putative TFBSs for Smad2/3 are present in the promoter region 2 kb upstream of the transcription start site of Fgf18.
source: Using JASPAR TF binding sites (TFBSs) predictions incorporated in the UCSC Genome Browser (Castro-Mondragon et al., 2022), we identified that several putative TFBSs for Smad2/3 are present in the promoter region 2 kb upstream of the transcription start site (TSS) (Figure 6A) and focused on the binding motif at chr11:33098353–33098362, which had the highest predicted binding score, since it is most likely to be the binding site (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by JASPAR TF binding site predictions shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Smad2/3 significantly binds to DNA fragments around the predicted binding motif at chr11:33098353–33098362 in the Fgf18 promoter region.
source: Using a Cut and Run assay for Smad2/3, we identified significantly greater binding Smad2/3 to DNA fragments around this binding motif when compared to IgG control (Figure 6B), suggesting direct binding of Smad2/3 to this predicted TFBS in the Fgf18 promoter region.
evidence: The claim is supported by Cut and Run assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Smad2/3 directly binds to the predicted TFBS in the Fgf18 promoter region.
source: Using a Cut and Run assay for Smad2/3, we identified significantly greater binding Smad2/3 to DNA fragments around this binding motif when compared to IgG control (Figure 6B), suggesting direct binding of Smad2/3 to this predicted TFBS in the Fgf18 promoter region.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the Cut and Run assay results.

claim: 4 hr of TGF-β1 treatment led to a significant increase of Fgf18 expression in soft palatal mesenchymal cells, which reduced when analyzed 18 hr post-treatment.
source: Consistent with previous studies which found that pSmad2 activity starts to decline around 5 hr following TGF-β1 treatment (Inman et al., 2002), we found that 4 hr of TGF-β1 treatment led to a significant increase of Fgf18 expression, which reduced when analyzed 18 hr post-treatment (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Fgf18 CRISPRi plasmid significantly attenuated the increase in expression of Fgf18 following TGF-β1 treatment compared with the control CRISPRi plasmid.
source: Compared with the control CRISPRi plasmid, Fgf18 CRISPRi plamid significantly attenuated the increase in expresssion of Fgf18 following TGF-β1 treatment (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The binding to the TFBS at chr11:33098353–33098362 in the Fgf18 promoter region is functionally required for the TGF-β-Smad2/3 signaling cascade to directly activate Fgf18 expression.
source: This finding suggested that the binding to this TFBS in the Fgf18 promoter region is functionally required for the TGF-β-Smad2/3 signaling cascade to directly activate Fgf18 expression.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the CRISPRi experiment results.

claim: One mechanism for cell-type-specific response to TGF-β signaling is through the cooperation with cell-type-specific master transcription factors, which enable TGF-β signaling to specifically affect the cell-type-specific genes bound by these master regulators.
source: The biological effects of TGF-β signaling are contextual (Morikawa et al., 2016). One mechanism for cell-type-specific response to TGF-β signaling is through the cooperation with cell-type-specific master transcription factors, which enable TGF-β signaling to specifically affect the cell-type-specific genes bound by these master regulators (Mullen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) mediated by Hic1, Creb5, Meox1, Etv5, Tbx15, Bach2, and Nr2f2 are most associated with perimysial fibroblasts.
source: We identified that gene regulatory networks (GRNs) mediated by Hic1, Creb5, Meox1, Etv5, Tbx15, Bach2, and Nr2f2 are most associated with perimysial fibroblasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by SCENIC analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hic1, Creb5, Meox1, Etv5, Tbx15, and Bach2 are more enriched and specific to the perimysial fibroblasts than other palatal mesenchymal populations.
source: The expression patterns of these genes in scRNAseq data indicated that Hic1, Creb5, Meox1, Etv5, Tbx15, and Bach2 are more enriched and specific to the perimysial fibroblasts than other palatal mesenchymal populations, and are thus more likely to be associated with the perimysial fibroblast-specific cell behaviors (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Creb5 has been reported to be required for TGF-β signaling to induce Prg4 expression during chondrocyte development.
source: Among the perimysial-associated factors, Creb5 has been reported to be required for TGF-β signaling to induce Prg4 expression during chondrocyte development (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Creb5 was most abundantly expressed in the perimysial fibroblasts, similar to that of Fgf18 and TGF-β signaling activity.
source: In vivo expression patterns further validated that, among these regulatory genes (Figure 6I–N), Creb5 was most abundantly expressed in the perimysial fibroblasts (Figure 6I), similar to that of Fgf18 and TGF-β signaling activity (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Creb5 expression was present in the palatal mesenchyme as early as E13.5, similar to TGF-β signaling activity and Fgf18 expression.
source: Moreover, unlike that of Tbx15, Creb5 expression was present in the palatal mesenchyme as early as E13.5, similar to TGF-β signaling activity and Fgf18 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Creb5 expression did not change in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mutant from E13.5 to E14.5, suggesting it is likely to function as a partner rather than a downstream target of the TGF-β signaling.
source: Since its expression did not change in the mutant from E13.5 to E14.5, it is likely to function as a partner rather than a downstream target of the TGF-β signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed expression patterns shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Creb5 is likely one of the candidates that may function cooperatively with TGF-β signaling to activate perimysial-specific signaling genes such as Fgf18.
source: We thus hypothesized that Creb5 is likely one of the candidates that may function cooperatively with TGF-β signaling to activate perimysial-specific signaling genes such as Fgf18.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the expression patterns and previous research.

claim: Reduction of Creb5 in soft palatal mesenchymal cells led to reduction of Fgf18 expression.
source: To test the function of Creb5, we first evlauated its role in regulating Fgf18 expression using E14.5 soft palatal mesenchymal cell culture and found that reduction of Creb5 in soft palatal mesenchymal cells led to reduction of Fgf18 expression (Figure 6O and P), indicating that Creb5 can regulate Fgf18 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6O and P.

claim: Creb5 can regulate Fgf18 expression.
source: To test the function of Creb5, we first evlauated its role in regulating Fgf18 expression using E14.5 soft palatal mesenchymal cell culture and found that reduction of Creb5 in soft palatal mesenchymal cells led to reduction of Fgf18 expression (Figure 6O and P), indicating that Creb5 can regulate Fgf18 expression.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the qPCR data.

claim: Reducing Creb5 significantly attenuated the increase of Fgf18 expression in soft palatal mesenchymal cells following TGF-β1 treatment.
source: To evaluate the cooperation of Creb5 and TGF-β signaling, we compared the increase of Fgf18 following TGF-β1 treatment with or without Creb5 reduction, and found that reducing Creb5 signficantly attenuated the increase of Fgf18 expression in soft palatal mesenchymal cells (Figure 6Q), suggesting that TGF-β signaling requires cooperation with Creb5 to efficiently activate downstream targets like Fgf18 in the perimysial fibroblasts.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6Q.

claim: TGF-β signaling requires cooperation with Creb5 to efficiently activate downstream targets like Fgf18 in the perimysial fibroblasts.
source: To evaluate the cooperation of Creb5 and TGF-β signaling, we compared the increase of Fgf18 following TGF-β1 treatment with or without Creb5 reduction, and found that reducing Creb5 signficantly attenuated the increase of Fgf18 expression in soft palatal mesenchymal cells (Figure 6Q), suggesting that TGF-β signaling requires cooperation with Creb5 to efficiently activate downstream targets like Fgf18 in the perimysial fibroblasts.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the qPCR data.

claim: TGF-β signaling activity (pSmad2), Creb5 and Fgf18 are also expressed in a similar pattern in the perimysial cells during the development of the masseter muscle.
source: Furthermore, we also found that TGF-β signaling activity (pSmad2), Creb5 and Fgf18 are also expressed in a similar pattern in the perimysial cells during the development of the other pharyngeal muscles, such as the first pharyngeal arch-derived masseter muscle (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), confirming the possibility that this TGF-β signaling and Creb5 cooperation in regulating perimysial signals, which we identified using the soft palatal muscle model, can plausibly be extended to other craniofacial muscles.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The TGF-β signaling and Creb5 cooperation in regulating perimysial signals can plausibly be extended to other craniofacial muscles.
source: Furthermore, we also found that TGF-β signaling activity (pSmad2), Creb5 and Fgf18 are also expressed in a similar pattern in the perimysial cells during the development of the other pharyngeal muscles, such as the first pharyngeal arch-derived masseter muscle (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), confirming the possibility that this TGF-β signaling and Creb5 cooperation in regulating perimysial signals, which we identified using the soft palatal muscle model, can plausibly be extended to other craniofacial muscles.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed expression patterns in the masseter muscle.

claim: Loss of Fgf18 in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice did not result in any obvious palatal shelf formation defects compared to the control mice at birth.
source: Unlike in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice, loss of Fgf18 in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice did not result in any obvious palatal shelf formation defects compared to the control mice at birth (Figure 7A–D), consistent with recent studies demonstrating that Fgf18 is not required for the development of mesenchymal cells themselves in the hard palate (Xu et al., 2016; Yue et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7 and citations to previous research.

claim: Fgf18 is not required for the development of mesenchymal cells themselves in the hard palate.
source: Unlike in the Osr2Cre;Tgfbr1fl/fl mice, loss of Fgf18 in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice did not result in any obvious palatal shelf formation defects compared to the control mice at birth (Figure 7A–D), consistent with recent studies demonstrating that Fgf18 is not required for the development of mesenchymal cells themselves in the hard palate (Xu et al., 2016; Yue et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The sizes of the soft palatal muscles of the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice appeared to be smaller than those of controls, which was especially obvious in the posterior part of the LVP.
source: In contrast, the sizes of the soft palatal muscles of the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice appeared to be smaller than those of controls, which was especially obvious in the posterior part of the LVP (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The reduction of LVP muscle size in Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice was confirmed by reduced muscle cross-section area and muscle volume.
source: This reduction of LVP muscle size was confirmed by reduced muscle cross-section area (Figure 7M–Q) and muscle volume (Figure 7R–V) in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice compared with the controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification and microCT data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The MyoD+ myogenic cells appeared comparable in the control and Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl LVP at E14.5.
source: While the MyoD+ myogenic cells appeared comparable in the control and Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl LVP at E14.5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E), the myogenic cells in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice started to appear progressively reduced compared to the control, and this difference became more apparent at E16.5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–J), confirming the role of Fgf18 in late-stage myogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The myogenic cells in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice started to appear progressively reduced compared to the control from E14.5, and this difference became more apparent at E16.5, confirming the role of Fgf18 in late-stage myogenesis.
source: While the MyoD+ myogenic cells appeared comparable in the control and Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl LVP at E14.5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E), the myogenic cells in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice started to appear progressively reduced compared to the control, and this difference became more apparent at E16.5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–J), confirming the role of Fgf18 in late-stage myogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The loss of functional Exon1C of Fgf18 is efficient in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl soft palatal shelves.
source: We also confirmed that the loss of functional Exon1C of Fgf18 is efficient in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl soft palatal shelves (Figure 7—figure supplement 1K–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by BaseScope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fgf18 may not be required for determining the fate of palatal mesenchymal cells themselves, but rather may serve as a paracrine molecule for the myogenic cell development.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that Fgf18 may not be required for determining the fate of palatal mesenchymal cells themselves, but rather may serve as a paracrine molecule for the myogenic cell development.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the findings in Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice.

claim: The myogenic cells in Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice and controls are rarely apoptotic at E14.5.
source: At this stage, the myogenic cells in Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice and controls are rarely apoptotic (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and D), but display proliferative activity in both mutants and controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Caspase 3 staining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The myogenic cells in Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice and controls display proliferative activity at E14.5.
source: At this stage, the myogenic cells in Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice and controls are rarely apoptotic (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and D), but display proliferative activity in both mutants and controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a significant reduction of proliferation of Myf5+ cells in Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice at E14.5.
source: We could see a significant reduction of proliferation of Myf5+ cells in Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C, F, and G), suggesting that loss of Fgf18 led to reduced myogenic progenitor proliferation in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice, which ultimately led to smaller muscle mass.
evidence: The claim is supported by BrdU labeling data and quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of Fgf18 led to reduced myogenic progenitor proliferation in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice, which ultimately led to smaller muscle mass.
source: We could see a significant reduction of proliferation of Myf5+ cells in Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C, F, and G), suggesting that loss of Fgf18 led to reduced myogenic progenitor proliferation in the Osr2Cre;Fgf18fl/fl mice, which ultimately led to smaller muscle mass.
